title: A Protocol for Real-time 3D Single Particle Tracking
protocol: Affix the 488 nm solid state laser to the optical table using a home-built aluminum mount with mounting holes.
Firmly attach the laser head to the metal mount for stability and heat dissipation.
Adjust the laser beam height and direction using dielectric mirrors.
Ensure the laser beam is parallel to the optical table.
Set the laser beam height based on the microscope platform.
Collimate the beam with a pair of lenses.
Choose focal lengths for the lenses carefully to avoid clipping by the aperture of the 2D-EOD.
Place a pinhole at the focus of the first collimation lens.
Calculate an appropriate size for the pinhole using the given formula: \(d = \frac{1.064\lambda f}{D}\).
Mount the pinhole on a 3D translation stage.
Adjust the position of the pinhole to be precisely at the focus of the first collimation lens.
Place a laser power meter after the pinhole.
Adjust the pinhole position in XYZ to maximize the power meter readout.
Block any observed diffraction ring with an iris before the 2D-EOD.
Put the Glan-Thompson polarizer after the second collimation lens to clean the polarization of the laser beam.
Rotate the polarizer to find maximum transmission with the power meter.
Use 2 EODs to deflect the laser in the X and Y directions.
Maximize the laser transmission by adjusting the yaw, pitch, and height of each EOD.
Align the two EODs with respect to each other using the alignment marker provided by the manufacturer on the side of each deflector.
Apply a test pattern to the controller of the 2D-EOD to inspect the output of the EOD.
Place a half-wave plate between the Glan-Thompson polarizer and the 2D-EOD.
Place a long focal lens after the 2D-EOD.
Place a sCMOS camera at the laser focus.
Turn on the 2D-EOD to generate the knight's tour.
Rotate the half-wave plate until an evenly square laser distribution is observed on the camera.
Install a pair of lenses (L3 and L4) after the 2D-EOD to expand the beam.
Relay the focal plane using another pair of lenses (L5 and L6).
Install the dichroic filter to reflect the laser towards the objective lens.
Align the laser to go straight through the center of the objective lens using two irises on the top and bottom of a long lens tube.
Install a 10/90 beam splitter by which 10% of light is reflected for imaging by an sCMOS camera.
Pass 90% of light through to the APD for tracking.
Align the APD.
Focus the laser onto a coverslip by the objective lens.
Put a coverslip at the objective focus and check the intensity of the APD readout.
Install the APD focusing lens after the beam splitter.
Position the lens such that the laser reflection from the objective goes through the center of the lens.
Optimize the APD position by adjusting the 3D position to maximize the intensity from the laser reflection on the coverslip.
Install a longpass fluorescence emission filter before the beam splitter.
Place the TAG lens between Figure 1: L4 and L5.
Adjust the yaw, pitch, height, and lateral position such that the beam passes perpendicularly through the center of TAG lens.
Dilute 190 nm fluorescent beads to ~ 5 × 10^8 beads/mL in PBS.
Add 400 µL of the diluted bead solution onto a coverslip and mount it on the sample holder of the piezoelectric stage.
Put a fixed particle sample on the microscope.
Turn on the laser, micropositioner controller, piezo nanopositioner controller, TAG lens controller, and EOD controller.
Run the piezo nanopositioner in closed loop.
Raster scan the sample in XYZ using a custom scanning software program.
Collect counts from the APD during raster scanning.
Drive the piezo nanopositioner with the custom scanning software program.
Perform position calculation during raster scanning.
Remove the fluorescence emission filter.
Use the laser reflection from the coverslip to maximize signal intensity by adjusting the Z position of the micropositioner.
Place the sample at the focal plane.
Replace the fluorescence emission filter.
Open the scanning program.
Set the initial scanning range and step size (e.g., 10 x 10 µm with a 200 nm step).
Locate a particle within the large scanning range.
Shrink the scanning range and decrease the step size (e.g., 2 x 2 µm with a 100 nm step) after finding the particle.
Click the 'scan' button to perform a 3D raster scan to find the fluorescent focus.
Connect to the TAG lens control software.
Power on the TAG lens sequentially.
Change the output trigger mode from 'RGB' to 'Multiplane'.
Change the output trigger mode back from 'Multiplane' to allow phase adjustment.
Set the output phase to 0°, 90°, and 270°.
Select the 68,500 Hz frequency setting.
Click 'advanced', 'setting'.
Change the 'Max. Freq(Hz)' of column 0 from 70,000 Hz to 71,500 Hz.
Click 'Save Calibration', 'Exit Calibration'.
Switch the resonance to another frequency (for example, 189,150 Hz).
Switch the resonance back to the 68,500 Hz frequency setting.
Gradually change the amplitude to 35%.
Click 'Lock Resonance'.
Unlock Resonance after the frequency is locked.
Input the scanning range of x, y, and z.
Click the 'scan' button to scan the sample in XYZ to move the particle through the moving laser spot.
Adjust the values of laser position (ck) used in the position estimation loop if necessary.
When the TAG lens controller is off, ensure that raster scanned particle images taken before and after installing the TAG lens look identical.
Perform fluorescent particle Z stack scanning by moving the objective using the z nanopositioner.
Tune the position of the TAG lens until there is no drift in the particle images in the XY plane along the Z direction.
Install a sCMOS camera to visualize particles while they are being tracked after all components have been installed and optimized.
Load a fixed fluorescent particle sample onto the microscope and run the tracking program to lock one particle in the objective focal volume.
Install the 100 mm focal length lens (L8) and sCMOS.
Adjust the sCMOS position so that the image of the particle is focused to the smallest and brightest spot.
Turn on laser.
Turn on micro-positioner controller.
Turn on piezo nanopositioner controller.
Turn on TAG lens controller.
Turn on EOD controller.
Run piezo nanopositioner in open loop.
Set TAG lens software according to step 3.2.
Open and run tracking software.
Set position estimation parameters to optimized values found in Section 3.
Remove fluorescence emission filter.
Use reflection of laser from coverslip to maximize signal intensity as a function of Z position of micropositioner.
Increase focus position by 15 µm after finding coverslip.
Place back the fluorescence emission filter.
Set the integral control constants starting at a low value.
Slowly increase the integral control constants until oscillations are observed in particle position readouts.
Adjust the integral control constants to 80% of the value causing oscillations.
Typical values for XY 'integral gain' are around 0.012 and for Z 'integral gain' around 0.004.
Set the tracking thresholds in 'Track Threshold' and 'Track Minimum'.
Start the tracking experiment by clicking 'Search' and 'Auto Track'.
Set the threshold for terminating tracking slightly higher than background level.
Set the threshold for triggering tracking about two times higher than background.
Here, the threshold for triggering tracking is 3 kHz.
The threshold for ending the trajectory is 1.5 kHz.
